Runtime hydration, Artifact issuance, and availability leases are specified in [Reference admission and availability](protocols/artifacts.md#reference-admission). ## Expressions and predicates Expression text and structured trees share one typed expression model. `Expression` produces a value of T; `Predicate` names a condition position requiring a boolean Expression, optionally nullable, not a separate value domain. Comparisons and boolean operations produce true, false, or null (the three-valued unknown). Storing the result preserves null. No string or number truthiness is admitted. A boolean field or function is directly usable as a condition. `if(p, TRUE, FALSE)` deliberately maps null to false; it is not the general representation of a boolean expression's value. | Position | true | false | null | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Value position, including `derive` | store true | store false | store null | | `filter`, aggregate filter | admit row | exclude row | exclude row | | `if`, `case` condition | select branch | do not select branch | do not select branch | | `assert_rows.where` | row satisfies assertion | assertion fails | assertion fails | | `count_if` | count | do not count | do not count | `count` counts non-null argument values, including false; `count_if` counts only true. Each consumer uses these rules without inserting a Program-level cast or changing the boolean expression's identity. The following table closes expression placement and lowering in 0.1: | Position | Admitted tree and context | Evaluation/lowering | | --- | --- | --- | | `derive` value | Common Expression over the input row, including pure profile calls | Canonical typed expression; conditional demand and per-expression envelopes preserved | | `filter`, `assert_rows.where` | Boolean Expression over the input row | Common evaluation followed by the condition-consumption rule | | Aggregate `expr` | Common row-local Expression | Each aggregate's filter first, expression only for its admitted rows, then null exclusion, distinct, and fold ([group](#group)) | | Graph/sequence conditions | Boolean Expression in the operation's property/event context | Same expression laws and profiles; Carrier scope remains operation-specific | | Effect `where` element | EffectPredicate over target fields ([Predicates](#predicates)) | Common decode followed by restricted selector validation; no scalar computation | An inadmissible expression or selector node MUST fail during check in either notation. Moving a subexpression to a separate step is valid only if its evaluation conditions, failure behavior, and resource bounds remain unchanged; a compiler MUST NOT evaluate an unselected branch by hoisting it before its conditional. Profile admission applies to every branch, but a pure profile does not require an author-visible intermediate step. Effect selector and invocation-value restrictions are not widened by expression composition. Source notation and precedence are in [Expression text](#expression-text); canonical representation, printing, and diagnostics in [Decoding, identity, and printing](#expression-decoding). Value families and their evaluation rules are in [Scalar expressions](#scalar-expressions) and [Decimal expressions](#decimal-expressions)–[Text, time, and regular expressions](#text-time); predicate structure and evaluation are in [Predicates](#predicates). ### Scalar expressions An expression or predicate position accepts expression text ([Expression text](#expression-text)) or the structured tree form. In the tree form, field references, literals, and parameters use `{field: ...}`, `{literal: ...}`, and `{$param: name}`. Text is decoded to the same tree before identity computation ([Decoding, identity, and printing](#expression-decoding)). Strings in non-expression positions, including inside `literal`, `meta`, requests, and template bodies, retain their declared meaning and are not recursively parsed as expressions. The Core scalar grammar contains: - arithmetic `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, and `modulo`; - boolean/comparison expressions, `case`, three-argument `if`, `coalesce`, and `nullif`; - `len`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `concat`, `safe_div`, `safe_divide`, `safe_add`, `safe_subtract`, `safe_multiply`, `safe_negate`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `asinh`, `acosh`, `atanh`, `pow`, `exp`, `ln`, `log`, `log10`, `abs`, `sign`, `round`, `trunc`, `greatest`, `least`, and `floor`; - the authoring-only string `template` form; - `lower`, `upper`, `trim`, `ltrim`, `rtrim`, `substring`, `left`, `right`, `lpad`, `rpad`, `split`, and literal `replace`; - `date_trunc`, `date_add`, and `date_diff`; and - explicit `to_number`, `to_string`, `to_boolean`, and `to_timestamp`; - `to_decimal`, `try_decimal`, `quantize`, and `decimal_divide`; and - closed `object`, homogeneous `array` and typed empty-array construction; - typed property/subscript access and type-preserving numeric `negate`. `coalesce` is a lazy expression, not a macro that evaluates a child twice. `template` is a deterministic authoring macro for ordinary messages and labels: ```yaml - derive: message: {template: "{name} is at risk — active users: {active_users_30d}"} ``` Each `{field}` placeholder MUST name one visible `string`, `number`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `timestamp`, or `date` field. The compiler MUST lower placeholders to canonical `to_string` followed by left-to-right strict `concat_strict`. The lowering uses no locale, host formatting, or expression evaluator. `{{` and `}}` emit literal braces. Unmatched braces, empty placeholders, unknown fields, and non-scalar fields are invalid. Null interpolation follows the `to_string` and `concat_strict` rules and therefore produces null. Parameters and nested expressions are not template placeholders; authors use the ordinary explicit expression grammar when those are required. `substring(value, start[, length])` MUST use the GoogleSQL STRING position rule in the common scalar owner: positive positions are one-based, zero and positions below negative input scalar length select the first scalar, other negative positions count from the end, and positions beyond the input select an empty string. An omitted length retains the suffix, zero length returns empty, and positive length retains at most that many Unicode scalars. Every supplied child evaluates once in value/start/length order; any NULL result propagates after all children succeed and before domain validation. A non-integer or unsafe start/length, or negative length, fails only when the non-null call is demanded. Index arithmetic is exact and clamped before addition. Retained scalars, including astral, combining, NUL and line breaks, remain unchanged. The result retains known input `max_codepoints` and `max_utf8_bytes`, drops `min_length`, and unions supplied operand nullability. The closed source body is `{substring: {value, start, length?}}`; omission is preserved in the corresponding machine body. SQL `SUBSTR` and `SUBSTRING` select this same operation, with the existing finite binary64 safe-integer range rather than the complete GoogleSQL INT64 domain. BYTES is not admitted. Substring has no text-time envelope/profile requirement; nested profile calls retain their own obligations, input preflight and selected resource limits. All scalar logical-work, live-value, output-byte, workspace, failure and cooperative cancellation requirements remain applicable. `left(value, length)` and `right(value, length)` MUST return at most the specified number of Unicode scalars from the corresponding end. Zero returns empty; a length at least the input scalar count returns the entire input. `lpad(value, length[, pattern])` and `rpad(value, length[, pattern])` MUST return exactly the requested scalar length. They truncate the original value to its leftmost requested scalars when the requested length does not exceed its length. Otherwise they prepend or append repetitions of the pattern, taking only the needed prefix of its final repetition. The omitted pattern is U+0020. An explicitly empty pattern is a domain failure even when no padding is needed. Every supplied child MUST evaluate once, left to right, before strict NULL propagation and then domain validation. A demanded, non-null call fails for negative, nonintegral or unsafe-integer lengths. Child failure identity and lazy branch demand remain unchanged. All lengths use ActQL finite binary64 safe integers; full GoogleSQL INT64, BYTES and collation remain unsupported. Unicode scalars, including astral characters, combining marks, NUL and line breaks, MUST remain unchanged without normalization or grapheme segmentation. Omission stays omitted; an implicit pattern expression is not inserted. Side slices retain input String maxima and drop minimum length. Padding drops input maxima because runtime padding can expand beyond them. All supplied operands contribute to result nullability. The existing scalar continuation owns cooperative counting, boundary location, exact output sizing and construction. Before output buffer allocation, all output logical bytes and workspace MUST be admitted. Retained operand roots, logical work, live values, control work and cancellation stay with the existing owners. `split(value[, delimiter])` MUST accept one STRING expression and an optional ordinary STRING delimiter expression, returning an Array of non-null String elements. The Array is nullable exactly when any supplied operand is nullable; untyped NULL takes the unique STRING signature at either position. The admitted domain is the existing finite, bounded String domain without implicit conversion, BYTES, regular-expression or collation overloads. An omitted delimiter is U+002C COMMA. Empty input produces one empty String, including with an empty delimiter; an empty delimiter on nonempty input produces one String per Unicode scalar. No normalization, case folding, trimming or grapheme segmentation is applied, including to astral characters, combining marks, NUL and line breaks. A literal match does not restrict the delimiter expression to a literal or parameter. If neither is known, or the addition is unrepresentable, omit `max_items`. Type derivation does not evaluate the value or delimiter expression or invent a minimum bound. Every supplied `split` child MUST evaluate exactly once, value before delimiter, before strict NULL propagation. A NULL value does not suppress a demanded delimiter failure. Preserve the first child failure and enclosing lazy demand; no secondary evaluator or Host splitting helper replaces the common owner. Omission remains distinct from explicit NULL or an explicit comma expression. Do not fold the node, reorder children or substitute the separately owned `split_part` profile. Raw signed-zero pairs (+0, +0) and (-0, +0) yield canonical positive zero, (+0, -0) selects positive pi, and (-0, -0) selects negative pi. Public canonical Number zero is positive, so public `atan2(0, 0)` is positive zero; the raw signed-zero diagnostic does not admit negative-zero wire values. Runtime domain checks do not narrow the static type or add a distinct numeric overload. Their literal wrappers use CellValue quoting, not expression decoding, template expansion or the mixed expression printer. Printing never interprets a cell payload as expression children, even when its keys resemble expression tags or parameter holes. Structured and text expressions may be mixed; both use the same tree validation and lowering. The canonical local_body referenced by `program_template` contains decoded expression trees, never expression-text nodes; string literal payloads remain string values. Decoding does not evaluate expressions, reassociate arithmetic, or infer semantic choices, and is not a Normalization Journal entry. Existing semantic completion and macro rules still apply to the decoded tree ([Deterministic completion](#completion)). Text and structured forms decoding to the same tree MUST have the same Program identity. Whitespace outside tokens, keyword case, and equivalent field quoting do not change that tree. Parentheses wrapping an existing subtree preserve its identity only when they do not change operator grouping or arity. An unparenthesized chain of `AND`, `OR`, or `||` decodes to one n-ary node (`and`, `or`, or `concat_strict`), in operand order; explicit grouping retains nesting. Arithmetic remains binary and is not reassociated. For example, `a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3` and `(a = 1 AND b = 2) AND c = 3` have different trees and Program identities. `coalesce` remains a dedicated node in both the canonical Program and the expression 0.1 canonical fragment. A canonical expression printer MUST preserve the tree, operand order, and literal values. It uses uppercase keywords, lowercase function names, unquoted non-reserved ASCII names where permitted, doubled quote escaping, AoA canonical number spelling, one space around infix operators, and comma followed by one space between arguments. It parenthesizes each operator application, prints conditionals as searched `CASE` or `if` according to their tree kind, and emits no trailing whitespace. Binary arithmetic and boolean expressions use the operator spellings in [Expression text](#expression-text); n-ary `and`/`or` print as a parenthesized chain. Membership prints a literal array as an `IN` list, or a parameter as its right operand. `not` prints as `NOT (p)` rather than rewriting the child predicate. For each text-representable canonical tree `t`, decoding its canonical printed text MUST yield `t`. Arrays print as `[a, ...]`; an explicitly typed empty array retains its structured form. The expression contract's pinned `regex_ast_contract` MUST govern regex AST representation and identity in preference to the inherited text-time profile's older string-literal AST representation. Matching, source grammar, flags and demand laws otherwise remain unchanged. Old string-valued literal nodes and range endpoints are rejected, not silently converted or assigned the new CID. A backend without this exact AST dependency and expression-contract support cannot produce an executable Plan for it; the old registry is not relabeled as supporting the new representation. Regex flags MUST be a string containing only `m` (anchors also match U+000A line boundaries) and `s` (dot also matches U+000A), each at most once, in either order. Omitted flags and the empty string both select neither flag. The `regex_extract` capture argument MUST be a nonnegative integer literal or an invocation parameter of number type. The `regex_replace` replacement argument MUST be a string literal or an invocation parameter of string type. Neither argument admits a row field or a computed expression, including a constant expression. Check validates the resolved non-null parameter value and its capture/replacement consistency with the admitted pattern before evaluation; declaration-only type checking does not discharge that obligation. The profile requires positive limits for input codepoints, pattern bytes, output bytes, and replacements. `regex_extract` requires an explicit capture index and returns null for no match; `regex_replace` applies a bounded left-to-right global replacement. Its closed replacement grammar uses `$$` for a literal dollar and `$1..$99` for captures; references to absent captures are rejected at Check, while an unmatched admitted capture expands to the empty string. The portable output ceiling accounts for every literal and repeated capture expansion. A limit breach fails atomically. Regex replacement tokenization MUST consume `$$` as one literal dollar, or a dollar followed by one ASCII digit `1..9` and, when present, one further ASCII digit `0..9` as a capture reference. Further digits are literal text: `$100` denotes capture 10 followed by literal `0`, not capture 100. Other dollar forms, including `$0`, `$01`, a bare dollar and `${1}`, are invalid. Backslash has no special replacement meaning. The canonical replacement AST coalesces adjacent literal text, including decoded `$$`, into one nonempty literal part; capture parts retain their order and repetition. An empty replacement has an empty parts array. Its literal UTF-8 byte total, capture reference count and maximum capture index (zero with no references) describe these parts, not the source spelling or a deduplicated set of captures. The operation/input matrix is closed: `split_part`, `utf8_truncate`, `try_number`, `parse_timestamp`, `regex_match`, `regex_extract`, `regex_replace`, `nfkc`, `case_fold`, and `try_timestamp` consume strings; `format_timestamp` consumes a timestamp. `parse_timestamp` preserves input nullability. `try_number` and `try_timestamp` have nullable output because input parse failure produces null. `nfkc` uses Unicode 16.0.0 compatibility normalization; `case_fold` uses full default C/F mappings, not locale-specific T mappings. Both return NFC. The profile pins the vendored Unicode table CID and derives expansion ceilings from those tables (18 decomposed scalars for NFKC, 4 for full folding/NFC per input scalar). `try_timestamp` uses the same UTC grammar as `parse_timestamp`. It MUST return null for invalid calendar/input text. An invalid pattern, bound breach, or engine failure MUST fail the operation rather than produce null. Null input propagates after the pattern has been checked. A quantified subexpression MUST consume at least one Unicode scalar on every successful match. Check rejects quantified anchors and any quantified capture, sequence, alternation, or repeat whose canonical AST is nullable; this keeps the grammar and the finite matcher state space identical across runtimes. Implementations MUST use the exact ActQL regex sets and boundaries below. Regex shorthand classes are exact ASCII sets: `\\d` is `0..9`, `\\w` is `A..Z`, `a..z`, `0..9`, and `_`, and `\\s` is TAB, LF, VT, FF, CR, and SPACE. Their uppercase forms are complements over the Unicode scalar universe. Dot excludes only LF unless `s` is set. With `m`, anchors use document or LF boundaries; CR remains an ordinary scalar, including in CRLF. An unmatched capture is null and expands to the empty string in `$1..$99` replacement. All ActQL strings and object keys MUST reject unpaired UTF-16 surrogates. ## Operations Each operation specifies its accepted Carrier, parameters, result, ordering, and failure conditions. No operation outside these closed contracts may execute as ActQL 0.1. ### Relation operations #### `filter` `filter` accepts the one explicit predicate grammar in [Predicates](#predicates): ```yaml - filter: and: - {eq: [{field: status}, {literal: open}]} - {gte: [{field: amount}, {literal: 100000}]} ``` Field-to-field and field-to-literal comparisons use the same binary form: ```yaml - filter: lt: - {field: score} - {field: required_score} - filter: lt: - {field: score} - {literal: required_score} ``` These are structured-form examples. Predicates also accept expression text ([Expression text](#expression-text)): `score < required_score` compares fields, while `score < 'required_score'` compares a field with a string literal. Operand expressions follow [Expressions and predicates](#expressions); names and literals are distinguished by syntax, not inferred from their values. `filter` lowers to `REL.where`. #### `select` Simple projection: ```yaml - select: [id, status, amount] ``` Projection with deterministic renaming: ```yaml - select: - opportunity_id: id - account_id ``` The map form means `{output_name: input_field}`. Projection order is semantic. `select` lowers to `REL.select`. `rename: {existing_name: new_name}` and `drop: [field, ...]` are convenience forms that retain the remaining complete input shape and lower directly to `REL.select`. They require a complete statically known field set. Duplicate output names, unknown fields, or dropping every field MUST fail during check. Given a complete input schema, check MUST accept `rename: {}` and `drop: []` as identity projections retaining every input field, including when the input schema itself has no fields. The prohibition on dropping every field applies to removing all fields from a nonempty input, not to preserving an already empty input. This does not admit `select: []`. Accepting an identity projection does not authorize deleting the authored operation or equating its semantic identity with omission of the operation; ordinary lowering and identity rules continue to apply. Repeated names in `drop` denote the same removal, not duplicate output fields. #### `sort` ```yaml - sort: - {score: desc} - {id: asc} ``` Each key MUST follow `OrderKey` in [Structural grammar (normative)](#structural-grammar) and specify `asc` or `desc`. The single-field map uses `last` for null placement where the AoA contract defines that completion as exact. The explicit `{field, dir, nulls}` form selects `first` or `last`; `nulls` is REQUIRED in that form. Null placement is independent of ascending or descending direction. `sort` lowers to `REL.orderByStable` for a nonempty authored key list. Check MUST accept `sort: []` as an identity operation preserving row values, multiplicity, schema, current order and existing evidence, including for empty input. An empty sort MUST NOT perform candidate-key sorting or establish new order evidence; it is an exception to the completion rule below. Acceptance MUST NOT authorize deleting the authored operation or equating its semantic identity with omission. Later consumers still apply their own order requirements, including any candidate-key completion permitted for `take`. Ordering ties that can affect a published Result or an order-sensitive operation MUST be resolved. For a nonempty authored sort, when the current relation retains a candidate key whose fields all have a portable order, the compiler MUST append missing key fields in ascending order as a deterministic identity tie-break and journal the completion. This does not invent a business field: it reuses proven identity evidence. Without a retained candidate key, the compiler MUST NOT invent a tie-break. `REL.orderByStable` MUST compare the supplied keys in their declared priority and preserve input-relative order for rows equal on all keys, without adding `valueCID` or any other implicit tie-break. The compiler MUST pass completed explicit keys and their completion record to lowering; the primitive does not perform candidate-key inference. An existing admitted total-order witness can justify stable tie resolution where the consuming operation's rules permit it; this is distinct from appending candidate-key fields. Stability alone MUST NOT promote physical input enumeration into deterministic total-order evidence. The empty-sort identity and evidence rules above remain unchanged. For nonempty `sort`, the compiler MUST prefer eligible candidate-key completion. If no eligible candidate key exists but an applicable admitted total input-order witness exists, it MUST resolve equal explicit-key tuples using only the relative order established by that witness. The sorted output MUST identify this sort as its order producer and retain the prior witness as a tie-resolution dependency, not copy the prior order as if the complete input sequence were unchanged. Projection hiding prior order fields does not itself invalidate a retained occurrence-order witness. With neither strategy available, the compiler MUST retain the order as unresolved and reject it at a boundary requiring total order. The checked strategy, authored keys, completion record or exact owned prior witness MUST be exposed to lowering without requiring order re-inference. This fallback is specific to `sort`; it does not relax the separate candidate-key requirements of `top_k` or `top_k_by`. #### `take` ```yaml - take: 20 ``` The object form is `take: {count: 20, offset: 40}`; its count member is named `count`, not `limit`. The count MUST be a positive safe integer. `take: n` and `take: {count: n, offset: 0}` normalize to the same closed object; `offset` defaults to zero and otherwise is a nonnegative safe integer. Skip that many rows, then retain at most count rows; an offset beyond the input yields empty output. `take` lowers to `REL.limit` with both values. The input MUST already have a proven stable order from `sort`, `top_k`, an ordered deterministic operation, admitted connector order evidence, or a retained candidate key that the compiler can order by and journal. Provider return order alone is not evidence and MUST NOT make `take` valid. #### `distinct` ```yaml - distinct: true ``` removes duplicate complete rows. A key projection MAY be written as: ```yaml - distinct: [customer_id] ``` Keyed distinct projects the declared keys before applying `REL.distinct`; it does not retain unspecified fields. A compiler MUST NOT choose a representative row for unspecified fields. Distinct MUST retain the first occurrence of each equal complete row in existing input order; keyed distinct applies this rule after the declared projection. It does not sort surviving rows or select values for fields omitted by that projection. Existing logical order is preserved, but provider arrival order without evidence does not become a stable-order proof through deduplication. This rule is independent of candidate-key propagation and does not introduce a non-null scalar identity for arbitrary complete rows. A keyed `distinct` list MUST be nonempty and contain no repeated field references, because it defines a projection with distinct output names. Check MUST reject `distinct: []` rather than reinterpret it as `distinct: true`. The list retains its authored projection order; these rules do not reject empty runtime input or impose a scalar-only schema on whole-row distinct. Fields selected by keyed `distinct` and fields in `dedupe_rows.by` MUST belong to the scalar or reference domains admitted by `KeyComparable`; nullable keys are permitted. Object, array, json and vector fields are not admitted as these explicit equality keys. This restriction does not apply to complete-row `distinct: true`. Authored ordering keys separately follow `AuthorOrderable`. Representative-row selection is a separate operation: ```yaml - dedupe_rows: by: [customer_id] order_by: - {updated_at: desc} - {source_id: asc} ``` `by` and non-empty `order_by` are REQUIRED. The operation keeps the first row in that order and fails an unresolved top tie; those are language invariants rather than authoring fields and are recorded in the Plan. The compiler lowers this to `REL.dedupeRows`. If two candidate rows for one key tie on every authored order key, execution MUST fail; implementation row order or CID MUST NOT silently choose the representative. Groups are emitted in ascending canonical typed key order, comparing the authored `by` tuple component by component with NULLS FIRST and the declared type's non-null comparison. This order is separate from canonical key encoding and from the authored order used to select each representative. Check MUST accept `dedupe_rows` with `by: []`, treating all input rows as one global partition. Its required nonempty `order_by` selects the first existing row; empty input yields zero rows, and a tie between top candidates fails under the same rule as any other partition. No representative row is synthesized. This differs from a global aggregate and from sort followed by take-one. Check MUST accept repeated `by` references while checking each reference's existence and applicable type requirements. The checked representation MUST retain their authored order and repetitions without preimage deduplication; repetition neither adds output columns nor proves uniqueness or resolves ties. #### `group` Aggregate calls MUST use the closed function-specific grammar below: `field` and `expr` are mutually exclusive, and only row-count `count` may omit both. String shorthand, `op`, function-name keys and `count_if.where` are not aliases. Check MUST accept an empty `aggregates` map and repeated `by` references while checking every input contract, reference and budget. An empty aggregate map produces only the grouping fields, once each in first-occurrence order; repeated conditions do not duplicate rows or strengthen uniqueness. With `by: []`, it produces one empty object even on empty input. Authored repetitions and the operation remain in the semantic source; no preimage deduplication, operation deletion or identity equivalence with another operation is implied. The `distinct` member accepts either boolean for `count(expr)`, `sum`, `avg`, `array_agg` and `string_agg`; only `false` for row-count `count`, `min` and `max`; and neither boolean for all other aggregate functions. No implicit cast is performed. A unique fixed immediate input domain supplies literal NULL with type evidence (for example number for `avg`, boolean for `count_if`, string for `string_agg`), but overloaded input domains and unresolved child computations receive no inferred type from the aggregate's result. `array_agg` constructs a non-null array of non-null root items, retaining nested nullability. Its item contract follows recursive value-construction rules: opaque `json` and reference types, including those hidden in arrays or objects, are not constructible here. In contrast, `first` and `last` select existing typed values and may retain structured, opaque JSON and reference contracts; their ordering keys independently satisfy AuthorOrderable. Aggregate capacity, order completion and numeric observation obligations are not discharged by static type checking alone. ```yaml - group: by: [customer_id] aggregates: event_count: {fn: count} total_amount: {fn: sum, field: amount} ``` Supported aggregate functions are `count`, `count_if`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `array_agg`, and the [ordered and statistical aggregates](#additional-aggregates). Every aggregate MUST have an output name. Every function except row-count `count` MUST name an input expression or field. `distinct: true` is admitted only for `count(expr)`, `sum`, `avg`, and `array_agg` and the explicitly admitted additional aggregates; it is invalid for row-count `count`, `count_if`, `min`, and `max`. The fixed evaluation order is each aggregate's filter, its argument expression on true rows only, null exclusion, canonical-value CID distinct, then stable fold. Argument expressions are not hoisted before their filters. Separate aggregates evaluate in canonical output-name order; each consumes rows in its specified input order. Every `array_agg` MUST declare its own non-empty `order_by`; these orders may differ between aggregates. The compiler applies each after its own filter, without imposing one aggregate's order or demand on another. Group results are canonically ordered by the group keys in ascending AoA order, including reference identity order ([Opaque reference values](#opaque-references)). The key tuple is compared lexicographically in authored `by` order, with NULLS FIRST independently at every component: two null components compare equal and comparison continues at the next component; a null component precedes every non-null value of its declared type. Non-null components retain their type-specific canonical order. This is group output enumeration, not the default null placement of authored `sort` or the input order of an aggregate. `group` lowers to `REL.groupBy` followed by that canonical group order. The final order also applies when `aggregates` is empty; primitive deduplication enumeration is not a substitute for it. Null group keys of the same declared type form one group. `by: []` is the global aggregate and emits one group even for empty input. `count` counts rows; `count` with an expression counts non-null expression values; `count_if` counts only true and excludes false/null. `sum`, `avg`, `min`, and `max` ignore null and return null when no non-null value exists. `min`/`max` require one `AuthorOrderable` type ([Lexical and ordering rules](#ordering)). `array_agg` excludes null, applies `distinct` equality by canonical value CID while retaining the first occurrence in the authored stable order. `array_agg.max_items` is an author guard as defined in [Author guards, resolved limits, and Plan facts](#resolved-limits), counting elements in each aggregate array after null exclusion and any distinct step. Its resolved limit uses input proof, Host policy, and any authored guard. Its order MUST retain a candidate key so equal authored keys cannot choose a row by provider enumeration. A breach MUST fail the aggregate operation without publishing a partial Relation or truncated array. For groups containing binary64 sum/avg, lowering preserves the same checked grouping and result contract but inserts typed numeric observation slots for those aggregate values. Exact aggregates remain AoA computation; replay uses the captured slot values. Describing group as `REL.groupBy` does not authorize recomputing an observed floating reduction on replay. ### Captured floating-point aggregates Binary64 `sum` and `avg`, including their group, window_group, pivot and analytic forms, use a compiler-inserted numeric observation boundary. Both local and remote reductions MUST capture the admitted result before any downstream filter, ordering, Result or Preview consumes it. Replay reuses that value, never a newly computed approximation. Determinism is over the ObservationSet including numeric observations, not merely over the original input rows. Placement may choose a Contract-admitted reduction algorithm with its declared rounding and error law; it cannot choose arbitrary opaque code. A numeric contract fixes contributors, input type, filter demand, NULL/distinct semantics, group/window identity, count, finite output, overflow and algorithm/error law. Wrong groups, counts, domains or demand are not numerical tolerance. The closed boundary does not authorize unrelated provider computation or additional egress. No universal epsilon is inferred. Cancellation in `[1e16, 1, -1e16]` can produce 0 or 1 under different reductions; differences are not necessarily one last bit. Numeric observations MUST bind the semantic aggregate slot, logical input artifact, post-filter contributor evidence, group/window key, NULL/distinct law, input type/count, adopted finite value, provider/kernel law and policy/cost evidence. Slot identity precedes response capture and excludes future Stage Invocation/Result CIDs. The logical Plan binds the aggregate and slot contract, not future physical parallelism or response bytes. Different fresh placements may change ObservationSet, Invocation and Result identities without changing Program identity; same-observation replay cannot. `count`, `count_if`, exact decimal sum, and a separately proved integer sum retain exact semantics and final public-domain checks. Integer evidence requires an admitted integer/range contract, not values that happen to look integral. Integer sums use exact accumulation; an admitted integer average requires an explicit result/rounding law. Decimal average is not introduced implicitly. Decimal scale zero remains an explicit exact route. Min/max, ordered strings, variance/percentile laws, VecA scores and graph means retain their own laws. Scalar binary64 arithmetic is unchanged. Money and exact decisions should use the explicit exact value domains, not assume approximate reduction invariance. #### `join` ```yaml - join: with: contracts kind: left on: - {left: organization_id, right: organization_id} - {left: account_id, right: crm_account_id} cardinality: many_to_one select: opportunity_id: left.id renewal_at: right.renewal_at ``` `with` names the right relation. `left` MAY explicitly replace the current relation. `kind` is REQUIRED and MUST be one of `inner`, `left`, `full`, `semi`, or `anti`. `on` MUST state one equality key or a non-empty array of equality keys; same-name field shorthand is permitted. Arbitrary non-equality conditions are not part of this join; bounded Cartesian products and temporal overlap use the separately specified `cross_join` and `interval_join` operations. Check MUST permit step-level `from` together with `join.left`: step `from` selects the main input first, then `join.left` replaces it as the actual left operand. Without step `from`, `join.left` replaces current and can establish the left operand when current is unset. Both explicit selectors MUST resolve to available Relation bindings under the ordinary name-scope rules; an invalid `from` is not ignored merely because `join.left` overrides its selection. The checked join's left input edge identifies the final selected operand, not the overridden binding. The join output becomes current as usual. Check MUST accept repeated equality pairs and repeated use of one side's field with different fields on the other side. Every pair is checked independently; the checked representation MUST retain the authored pair order and repetitions. Acceptance does not authorize deduplication of the operation's semantic preimage. `cardinality` is an OPTIONAL validation assertion, not output semantics. It is one of `one_to_one`, `many_to_one`, or `one_to_many`; it asserts uniqueness of both sides, the right side, or the left side respectively. A violated uniqueness assertion MUST fail before a result is accepted. This failure behavior is a language invariant, not an authoring policy. When `cardinality` is omitted, the compiler MUST derive it only when candidate key evidence proves the join-key tuple unique on the left, the right, or both. Uniqueness on both sides proves `one_to_one`; uniqueness only on the right proves `many_to_one`; uniqueness only on the left proves `one_to_many`. When neither side is proven unique, cardinality remains unproven; the compiler MUST NOT infer `many_to_many`. A derived cardinality and its candidate-key proof, including any SourceView Contract CID on which it depends, belong to the Compiled Plan and are not source normalization. An authored cardinality is recorded as an author assertion and requires the same fail-on-violation runtime check. Static uniqueness evidence and the authored assertion are combined per side. A proven unique right side together with an asserted unique left side yields `one_to_one`; the Plan retains both sources of evidence. The assertion does not discard a stronger static proof. Omitted `null_key` has the fixed SQL-style `no_match` language law and creates no normalization entry. Explicit `null_key: no_match` is legal and normalizes to the same canonical form as omission; `null_key: fail` is the sole authored override and rejects a null key component on either input. `max_output_rows` is an author guard as defined in [Author guards, resolved limits, and Plan facts](#resolved-limits), counting joined output rows. Its resolved limit uses safe join-cardinality transfer over both inputs, current Host policy, and any authored guard. A breach MUST fail the join before publishing its output Relation. A breach publishes neither a partial Artifact nor a partial output Relation. Before an Artifact serialization barrier is admitted, the input Relation MUST have either a compiler-proven candidate key or a total stable ordering witness from an algebra contract. When a candidate key closes authored ordering ties, its omitted fields are appended ascending and journaled. Authored `order_by` alone cannot prove that ties are impossible. The output fields are exactly `artifact_ref`, `media_type`, `size_bytes`, `logical_name`, and `row_count`. The barrier input CID is derivation evidence, not business data. Only the host Artifact Store may issue the `artifact_ref`. ActQL source MUST NOT contain bytes, base64, storage locators, or an author-supplied content CID. Upload, attachment, and resumable transfer remain Connector-owned typed `command` Effects over the resulting `artifact_ref`. `serialize` creates an Invocation-scoped immutable Artifact. Workspace persistence, retention, and later deletion are not serialization semantics; they require an explicit typed store/upload Effect or Run Graph policy. CSV serialization is byte-faithful and performs no implicit spreadsheet formula escaping. Authors apply any business transformation before serialization. ### Artifact-backed acquisition ActQL has no media profile and no `extract_text`, `transcribe`, `ocr`, or provider-feature operation family. A captured PDF, image, or audio object is an `artifact_ref`; already extracted information may be read as a typed Relation. A keyed SourceView accepting an ArtifactRef is subject to exactly the same observation classification as a direct SourceView ([Connector SourceViews](#sourceviews)). It may read existing structured results or capture bytes. Newly interpreting a document requires a registered extraction profile; [SourceView transformation profiles](protocols/contracts.md#sourceview-transformations) currently registers none. Naming a View `text` or `transcription` does not authorize that work. Accepted MIME types, full-artifact requirements, byte limits, schema, completeness, data policy, and egress scope remain explicit Contract terms. An asynchronous provider flow that requires submit, wait/poll, and result fetch is not one hidden acquisition. Submission is a typed Command, waiting and outcome routing belong to the Run Graph, and the completed bytes or result are captured by a later SourceView. Model-based extraction uses an explicitly admitted ModelTask, not a hidden SourceView callback. Local byte transformations likewise require a registered profile. Modality alone MUST NOT select execution semantics. ## Named Results and Effect declarations ### Named Results This subsection defines stage-local `ResultDefinition` values. Program-root Results instead use the explicit Stage Result export grammar in [Stages](#stages). They inherit this closed Result contract and cannot reselect its fields. Every ActQL Program MUST declare a map of closed named `results`. An empty Program-root `results` map is permitted only when the Program contains at least one Effect validated by the common Checker, including its input, target, Mapping and Capability requirements. A stage with no local Results likewise requires an Effect. A Program with neither public Results nor Effects MUST be rejected. SQL spelling, Connector names and self-declared flags do not establish this exception. Checked Effects are execution-plan roots, including when there are no public Results. Execution, approval, recovery and release MUST retain their ordinary owner contracts; no hidden public Relation is generated. Unapproved, unknown commit and unresolved Effect states MUST NOT be treated as successful completion. Recovery reconciles the original operation and its saved receipt; it MUST NOT automatically resend an unknown operation. Private Table capture preserves absence separately from NULL without relaxing the normal Named Result all-Required contract. Releasing or cancelling the origin Run does not delete a committed persistent Table. Each member is a logical publication boundary and may be consumed by an Effect or retrieved independently after the Run has materialized it: ```yaml steps: - top_k: k: 20 by: [{score: desc}, {product_id: asc}] as: ranked_candidates results: response: from: ranked_candidates fields: [customer_id, product_id, score] order_by: - {customer_id: asc} - {score: desc} - {product_id: asc} ``` A named Result is a Relation. A `ResultDefinition.from` is REQUIRED and MUST name an authored dataflow binding: a declared input, an explicit step `as`, or an explicitly named multi-output port in the completed pipeline. Compiler-generated AoA step IDs are not ActQL source names and MUST NOT be accepted there. `fields` is REQUIRED. It closes the data published by the Result, including delivery and Effect consumption; the compiler does not widen that boundary when an upstream Relation gains a field. Optional `order_by` belongs to the named Result, not to serialization. A Result MAY select a raw join output using exact provenance-qualified names such as `fields: [left.id, right.id]`; its `order_by` uses the same reference rules against the source before projection. The Result schema and published column names MUST retain the selected qualification and provenance without implicitly stripping prefixes, merging same-named fields, or reinterpreting them as authored flat names. This does not permit dotted authored source fields or nested-property selection through `fields`. Result `fields` introduces no alias syntax. A consumer that requires flat fields MUST be supplied a Result whose required fields have been explicitly flattened upstream with join `select`, a select alias, or `rename`; it cannot silently flatten them at the consumption boundary. All ordinary Result type, order and publication checks still apply. If present, result `order_by` is applied before its field projection and lowers to `REL.orderByStable`. `fields` lowers to `REL.select`. The compiler MUST verify that every ordered and projected field exists and reject an authored typed order key unless its type is `AuthorOrderable` ([Lexical and ordering rules](#ordering)). It MUST report the exact Result schema when statically known, including for empty runtime results. Columns-only evidence cannot prove an order-key type; such inputs retain the deferred `AuthorOrderable` obligation of [Lexical and ordering rules](#ordering), while generated or typed non-scalar order keys are rejected during planning. Every named Result MUST have a proven total deterministic order at its publication boundary. This rule applies even when no delivery is requested or the Result is consumed only by an Effect, because later delivery selection is not part of the checked Program. Relation identity is a set of independently proven candidate keys; ordering is a separate witness. When a candidate key closes authored ties, missing key fields are appended to the Plan's ordering, not authored source ([Deterministic completion](#completion)). Result order is resolved in this priority: 1. Apply authored `order_by`, completing ties under [Deterministic completion](#completion). 2. Otherwise preserve an existing total stable ordering witness, including after a projection that hides its original order fields. 3. Otherwise order by the eligible candidate key selected by [Deterministic completion](#completion). 4. Otherwise order ascending, nulls last, by all projected fields in declared field order, if every field is `CanonicalOrderable` ([Lexical and ordering rules](#ordering)). 5. Otherwise reject the Result. For authored Result order, checking MUST first apply eligible candidate-key completion. If no eligible key is available, a retained total stable ordering witness MAY resolve ties by stable sorting: authored terms remain primary and the witness orders only rows equal on all those terms. This does not replace authored order with the inherited sequence. If neither is available, a retained, checked Graph edge identity from `edge_rows` MAY complete authored Result order. All three identity components (`src`, `dst`, `rel`), or their provenance-preserving aliases, must remain available. Select and append missing components by the canonical completion algorithm, ascending with nulls last; authored terms remain primary. The nullable label is part of Graph identity, not a non-null Relation candidate key. This evidence is conditional on the exact Graph producer's successful admission and whole-edge identity uniqueness; a row schema or physical edge enumeration cannot supply it. Projection that loses an identity component loses this completion evidence. This rule does not apply to Results without authored order, scalar identity selection or omitted `infer.key`. Without any of these witnesses, reject; projected-field fallback applies only when authored `order_by` is absent. Retained execution and admission obligations of the supporting witness still apply. No lower-priority rule overrides a higher-priority one. Physical input enumeration order MUST NOT break ties. If any Effect consumes a Result, checking MUST derive a machine-only evidence policy with `sensitivity: private`, retention class `authority-evidence`, and encryption required. The effective data and retention policies MUST satisfy that evidence policy and every constraint inherited from the Result's fields and provenance; where constraints on one dimension are ordered, the more restrictive value applies. This rule is not an author-visible `visibility` or retention field. ### Private Table inputs A stage may declare private `table_inputs` alongside its ordinary `results`. For example, `table_inputs: {material: {from: rows, fields: [id, p]}}` closes an authored Relation binding for one whole-Table operation, and that stage's Table `store` refers to it with `from: {table_input: material}`. This is a structured Program boundary; it adds no SQL syntax or public delivery format. Ordinary Result-backed all-Required Table inputs remain valid. Checking MUST resolve a Table input's authored `from` binding and nonempty, duplicate-free `fields` against the exact stage pipeline, reject unknown names and surplus declaration keys, and derive a closed schema from those selected fields including independent presence and nullable contracts even for empty input. A private Table input MUST remain distinct from ordinary Named Results and be consumed only by a Table-capable `store` in its declaring stage, with no Result export, downstream Result import, mixed `result`/`table_input` source, or implicit conversion to an all-Required Result. Capture MUST retain missing, explicit NULL and present values, exact source occurrence, field projection and schema through the existing Relation, Store and Effect input owners, without NULL filling, inferred presence guarantees, or Table writes before approval and current authority. The authored Table declaration and source choice MUST bind Stage/Program and operation identity; a consumer without the checked private input, completed capture and Table capability rejects it rather than treating it as a source-free Store or ordinary Result, while structural acceptance alone grants no execution, publication or commit authority. ### Effect declarations Effects are declarative, reviewable intent. Evaluating the computational part of an ActQL program MUST NOT apply an Effect. Proposal and commit are separate runtime phases; the Host MUST complete current preflight and any required Checkpoint Resolution before commit. Effect declarations lower directly to AoA `EFFECT.plan` as defined in [AoA fragments and algebra lowering](#algebra-lowering). ActQL 0.1 defines these closed effect kinds: ```text create update upsert delete command store ``` The full form is: ```yaml effects: mark_for_review: update: target: connector://crm/main/Opportunity mapping: mapping:crm.opportunity.v1 from: {result: crm_updates} match: target_field: Id result_field: opportunity_id set: NeedsReview: {literal: true} RiskScore: {field: risk_score} ``` The nested effect-kind key is the only ActQL 0.1 spelling. A sibling `kind` field is rejected rather than treated as an alias. The kind determines its authority class: - `create` appends and MUST NOT address existing rows; - `update` changes only addressed existing rows and MUST NOT create; - `upsert` may create or update against a declared mapping key; - `delete` removes only addressed rows and carries no field changes; - `command` invokes one Connector-owned typed provider operation against named-result `resource_ref` values; it is not arbitrary HTTP or generic CRUD; - `store` persists one declared named result, or one private Table input for a Table-capable Mapping. Every data effect MUST explicitly declare `target` and a typed-qualified Mapping Contract reference in `mapping`. Every command MUST explicitly declare a ResourceRef result field and Command Contract. Effect `max_items` is an author guard as defined in [Author guards, resolved limits, and Plan facts](#resolved-limits), constraining the kind-specific scope units in [Preview strength, scope, and freshness](execution.md#preview-strength). Its resolved limit uses Result or literal scope proof, Contract ceiling, Host policy, and any authored guard. Preview MUST enforce that limit on the complete resolved scope before creating an Effect Commit Checkpoint or dispatching a mutation. The runtime derives deterministic apply and row idempotency keys from the exact Effect Preview, resolved Contract, Effect member identity, target identity, operation, and intended change. The author does not name an idempotency namespace. Permissions are not Program vocabulary. The compiler and preview derive the exact permission set from the resolved Mapping or Command Contract and expose it in the checked Plan and review projection. Approval policy is not Program vocabulary. Execution-account configuration and, for delegated decisions, the Host decide Effect authority; Mapping and Command Contracts declare exact technical permission requirements, not approval policy ([Account authorization routing](execution.md#policy-routing)). A Program MUST NOT author an `approval`, `review`, `allow`, `deny`, or `checkpoint` key as Effect policy; such a key is invalid rather than a request to weaken or strengthen authority. `on_item_failure`, when present, MUST be `continue`; omission is the sole canonical spelling for the fixed fail-fast behavior. The resolved failure semantics MUST appear in the Plan and authority summary. ActQL 0.1 treats the Effects within each stage as one unordered intent set derived from the same Stage Invocation. Member source order is not execution order; the enclosing stage array does guarantee success-dependent order. The set provides no cross-member or cross-Connector atomicity, effect-to-effect order, distributed transaction, compensation graph, or Saga execution. Each member consumes at most one named result. A result-correlated member (`from: {result: name}` with `id`, `match`, or the upsert `key`; `create` and `store` from a result; every `command`) consumes exactly one. A target-addressed member (`ids`, `external_id`, `where`, or `create` with `payload`) consumes none. No member consumes another member's outcome within that same stage. Within one member, `on_item_failure` applies to its stable row sequence: `halt` stops that member after the first failed row and marks its remaining rows unattempted; `continue` attempts the remaining rows. Failure of one member does not suppress another independent member under the set's fixed `attempt_all` apply policy. A host apply receipt MUST distinguish every member and every applied, accepted, unknown, failed, or unattempted outcome. `compensate` is invalid in ActQL 0.1 rather than an underspecified promise. Before preview succeeds, the runtime MUST derive a structured write footprint for every member. Exact targets in the same provider boundary and identity scheme cannot overlap, even when different fields of the same row are written. A create collection footprint may coexist with updates only with admitted proof that planned keys are disjoint or that allocation cannot reuse existing keys. Without such proof collection overlap remains a conflict. An opaque footprint cannot be combined without a contract proving independence. Different Command payloads alone are not such a proof; a declared append capability may be. An identity-scheme mismatch within the same provider boundary is unprovable and therefore rejected. Authors cannot provide free-form conflict domains or waive this check. `update` and `delete` MUST use exactly one selector: ```yaml id: output_id_field match: target_field: Id result_field: opportunity_id ids: [literal_id_1, literal_id_2] external_id: {field: external_key, value: ACME-1} where: - {eq: [{field: status}, {literal: archived}]} ``` `id` is the preferred shorthand for reading primary-key IDs from one named result field and therefore requires `from: {result: name}`; the resolved mapping contract supplies the target primary-key name. `match` is not an alias for `id`: it carries an additional auditable assertion naming the target field, so its authority contract and ActQL CID remain distinct even when both forms emit the same AoA effect plan. In ActQL 0.1 `match.target_field` MUST equal the connector mapping contract's single declared primary key. The result key and target key MUST both be scalar, unique, and non-null. A missing target, duplicate result identity, duplicate target identity, non-primary target match, or identity-type mismatch MUST fail before preview succeeds. ActQL performs no implicit string/number coercion for identity matching; any permitted conversion must be explicit in the resolved mapping contract. `where` is a non-empty array of [Predicates](#predicates) predicates combined by conjunction. Its `{field: name}` operands address fields of the target Resource under the resolved Mapping Contract; they do not refer to an input Relation or named Result. Literal and parameter operands follow [Predicates](#predicates). Only a target row for which the conjunction is strictly true is selected; false and three-valued unknown do not select it. Arbitrary scalar expressions are not selector operands. Literal `ids`, `external_id`, and `where` address the target directly and MUST NOT declare `from`. The compiler MUST NOT infer a selector. `create` and ordinary `store` consume `from: {result: name}` unless create uses an explicit object `payload`; Table `store` may instead consume its stage's closed private `from: {table_input: name}`. `upsert` requires `from: {result: name}`, an explicit result-side `key`, and a non-empty `set` map. The mapping contract supplies the possibly differently named target-side single primary key. The runtime MUST correlate those two fields, MUST NOT assume they share a name, and MUST NOT copy the remaining result row into the target implicitly. `update` requires a non-empty `set` map. `delete` carries no field changes. A step alias is an internal dataflow node; an Effect may consume it only after stage-local `results`, or `table_inputs` for Table `store`, exposes a closed contract for it. A command consumes one named result. Its `target.field` MUST be a value-level `resource_ref` whose kind equals the Command Contract target kind. Each `input` member is exactly `{literal: ...}` or `{field: ...}` and is validated against the closed Connector-owned input contract. Unknown, missing, nullable, vector-dimension, ArtifactRef-media, and ResourceRef-kind mismatches fail during check or preview. The target field may be projected away only by making the command invalid; receipt-only lineage cannot restore it. An `update` or `upsert` change value is either a literal or a field from its correlated result row: ```yaml set: NeedsReview: {literal: true} RiskScore: {field: risk_score} Reason: {field: risk_reason} ``` The complete payload of an Effect `{literal: value}` retains its source keys as specified in [Source representation](#source-representation). After the target contract is checked, a JSON payload preserves those exact data keys; a typed Object applies its existing field-name normalization, collision rejection and closed-contract matching. Neither interpretation changes the already-bound source identity. Member names within the payload do not select a type, and an object containing `$json` remains authored data. This rule adds no `typed_literal` alternative to `EffectValue` and does not expand Values types. All literal values use the explicit `{literal: value}` form. Bare values are rejected with a deterministic explicit replacement and MUST NOT be interpreted from schema likelihood. A bare Effect value MUST be rejected before lowering. Its diagnostic MUST expose only explicit `{literal: ...}` and schema-valid `{field: ...}` repairs. Check MUST NOT guess between those meanings. `{field: name}` requires `from: {result: name}` and a result-correlated selector (`id`, `match`, or the upsert key). Check MUST reject unknown result fields. Preview MUST reject missing row values, target fields not declared by the resolved mapping contract, incompatible target types, target primary-key mutation, and duplicate row identity. It MUST compute separate strength-appropriate state evidence and a target guard for every correlated row under [Preview strength, scope, and freshness](execution.md#preview-strength). ## Checking and canonical planning ### Validation For a Program containing every required semantic choice, checking SHOULD succeed without an authoring repair. If one complete repair is unique and semantics-preserving, the checker MUST return that replacement. If several meanings remain possible, it MUST return stable explicit candidates rather than select a meaning. Diagnostic representation is specified in [Diagnostic documents](protocols/contracts.md#diagnostic-documents) and [Diagnostic compatibility profiles](protocols/contracts.md#diagnostic-profiles). Checking and planning MUST NOT execute source text, import modules, access the network, or resolve external connection authority. A source builder is subject to the same validation and canonical lowering contracts as textual source; it cannot bypass them with callbacks or embedded code. For supported profiles, planning MUST parse, elaborate, validate, and lower far enough to detect source, Carrier compatibility, arity, field, identity, ordering, and effect-scope errors without running the computation. Unsupported-profile rejection follows [Conformance profiles](conformance.md#conformance-profiles). Machine-readable diagnostics MUST include: ```text code path message ``` and SHOULD include, when known: ```text current_shape available_results replacement candidates allowed_keys operation_signature ``` A `replacement` is permitted only when one complete repair is semantically unique. When multiple repairs are possible, `candidates` MUST contain stable, complete alternatives and no replacement may be applied automatically. ### Deterministic completion The compiler MAY insert structure only when the result is type-unique and semantics-preserving. ActQL 0.1 permits: - previous-result wiring in a linear pipeline; - sole-input selection when exactly one input exists; - sole-SourceView selection under [Connector SourceViews](#sourceviews); - generated AoA step identifiers; - object-predicate expansion; - relation/carrier bridges required by `row_window`, `window_events`, `graph`, `reach`, and `nearest`; - graph branch projection and explicit distinct; - restoration of authored graph/vector identity names; - Result ordering and projection declared by each ResultDefinition; - the sole compiler-proven `infer` candidate key when `key` is omitted; - a retained declared identity as a stable tie-break or carrier identity. Whenever a rule permits choosing a candidate key, use this canonical algorithm: retain only keys whose fields remain available and satisfy the use's type and nullability requirements; sort each key's fields in canonical code-unit order; deduplicate identical tuples; then order tuples by field count, followed by lexicographic field sequence, and select the first. Append missing order fields ascending with nulls last. This selection applies to Result order, tie-break completion, eligible carrier identity completion, and preferred-identity summaries. A rule requiring a *sole* candidate (such as omitted `infer.key`) still rejects multiple candidates; canonical selection does not waive that rule. Reference fields are eligible for canonical ordering completion. Whenever ordering completion is required, the compiler MUST apply the algorithm above without excluding a key solely because it contains reference fields. Author-order restrictions apply to source before completion. Generated reference ordering belongs in the Plan and completion evidence, not an authored order key. Source printers, repair, and migration MUST NOT write it back as an author-selectable reference order or expose a source flag to bypass the rule. The compiler MUST NOT infer: - join kind or business join key; - fixed versus sliding versus session windows; - event-time versus processing-time fields; - an approximate external search in place of exact VecA; - vector metric; - traversal direction; - a business tie-break; - effect kind, effect scope, or approval policy; - one of multiple structurally compatible inputs. Fields with exactly one admitted meaning are not authoring vocabulary. Their values are language laws, not choices for the checker to infer. Optional validation assertions, including join cardinality, remain author choices even when existing evidence already entails them. Grammar decoding, including expression text ([Decoding, identity, and printing](#expression-decoding)), precedes these rules and is not a source completion. Every semantic source completion or macro expansion MUST appear in a stable normalization journal with source path, authored form, resulting canonical form, and rule identifier. Fixed operation semantics—such as SQL-style null non-match for an ordinary join, fail-fast Effect member execution, directed graphs, exact nearest-neighbor search, closed-open windows, first-row deduplication, fail-on-tie behavior, and lexicographic shortest-path ties—are language laws, not source completions. They MUST appear in the canonical Plan node and MUST NOT produce normalization entries. Facts derived from type, identity, or an external Contract are Plan proofs and MUST bind the evidence CID on which they depend; they likewise MUST NOT appear as source normalization. ### Normalization Journal The identity-bearing journal has version `actql-normalization-journal/0.1` and contains `rule_catalog_cid`, canonical `entries`, and `journal_cid`. Every entry has exactly `path`, `rule`, `authored`, and `canonical`. Paths use the declared RFC 9535-compatible JSONPath subset; rule IDs MUST exist in the frozen `actql-normalization-rule-catalog/0.1`. Entries are ordered by path, rule, authored bytes, then canonical bytes using the ActQL code-unit order. The journal CID is computed over `{version, rule_catalog_cid, entries}`. Compiler-specific notes or prose may accompany a journal only as non-semantic presentation and are excluded from its CID. Two implementations claiming the same normalization-rule catalog and check evidence MUST emit byte-identical semantic entries and journal CID. An implementation with different internal pass names maps them to the normative rule IDs rather than exposing those names as language semantics. ### Generated identifiers AoA steps generated from ActQL source receive deterministic identifiers based on document order and preferred operation names. Generated identifiers are not part of the ActQL authoring surface. There is no alias-equivalence class in ActQL source: operation, parameter, expression, and binding names use exactly their registered spelling. ### AoA fragments and algebra lowering ActQL source vocabulary, AoA registry vocabulary, and Executable Plan node vocabulary are three disjoint namespaces: ```text ActQL algebra form --lowers to--> AoA operation in an AoA Fragment ActQL boundary form --compiles to-> typed barrier node AoA Fragments + typed barriers ----> ActQL Executable Plan ``` An ActQL operation name describes the author-visible action. An AoA operation identifier names the canonical computation primitive selected by lowering. Lexical equality between those names is neither required nor semantic: for example, ActQL `filter` lowers to AoA `REL.where`. AoA identifiers such as `REL.where` are not ActQL source spellings and are rejected as unknown ActQL operations. The normative mapping below is the only connection between the two namespaces. Source names express author-visible actions rather than IR wiring; the generated operation inventory exposes their canonical mappings. Every fragment MUST satisfy the pinned AoA registry's sort compatibility, arity, cycle, dangling-reference, operation-parameter, and output validation contracts. A program without a boundary form executes those validated AoA Fragments directly. When an acquisition or Artifact boundary form is present, the compiler instead binds the validated fragments and content-addressed typed barriers into one `actql-executable-plan/0.1` envelope. The envelope is an ActQL protocol artifact, not ActQL source, not AoA IR, and not another authorable language. It has no authorable control flow and does not reinterpret AoA semantics. Failure to lower completely is a validation failure; a compiler MUST NOT emit a partially executable plan. #### Canonical binding of additional operations The added mappings specify required registry contracts, not permission to invoke unregistered kernel exports. The admitted registry and expression extension identities in the Check Environment bind these operations and their complete parameter, type, numerical and failure laws. An implementation without those contracts cannot issue a runnable Plan for the operation. Registration/implementation status is not a different source meaning. No physical indexes, hash tables, runtime batch partition or evaluator caches appear in this graph. Existing bridge lowering remains as specified above. Input references are current input first, then with for binary operations; mean_graphs uses its declared graph list; RRF uses current then its with list; text_rank uses corpus then queries; subgraph and shortest_path append named selector Relations in nodes/source/target slot order when present. Generators without referenced inputs have an empty input list. Repeated references keep their list positions. It does not assert that preflight has run, authorize input acquisition or insert capacity policy into Unit Definition identity. ### Canonical identities ActQL uses distinct identities rather than overloading one CID. Stage Definition CIDs bind stable stage IDs and local semantics without the enclosing Program CID. Program semantics bind their ordered descriptors, parameters, imports and exports; Program Definition adds the root ID. Node-local semantic identities never include the enclosing Program revision, transitively or directly. The graph membership envelope binds both sides separately. No definition hashes its containing Program or future observations. The following invocation/plan/manifest identities apply to an extracted single-unit Program; its Program Definition is the local Unit Definition, not the enclosing multi-node Program revision. The graph output index aggregates node history without new Invocations: - `source_text_hash` is non-semantic provenance over authored bytes; - `program_semantics_cid` is the CID of the canonical unbound ActQL semantic envelope, excluding authored `id` and every allowed presentation-only `meta` object; - `program_definition_cid` binds the authored authority-bearing `id` to that semantics CID; - `authoring_context_cid` identifies the separately extracted metadata sidecar bound to that Program Definition; - `check_environment_cid` binds the exact evidence bundle used by check; - `parameter_values_cid` binds one canonical typed value map using the [Parameter value identity projection](protocols/contracts.md#parameter-value-projection); - `invocation_template_cid` binds Program Definition CID, Parameter Values CID, Check Environment CID, and the fact that runtime sources remain unbound; - `executable_plan_cid` binds the complete graph and execution material ([Typed barriers and Plan Documents](#plan-documents)), including fragments, barriers/wiring, Results, effects, governing facts, resolved limits, source-state requirements, and semantic contract identities; - `compiled_plan_cid` identifies the compilation envelope below, including `executable_plan_cid`; it is not an alias for the main AoA logical CID; - `prepared_invocation_cid` binds one bound Invocation Template and Compiled Plan to an authenticated execution context, current Host policy decision, and expiration without restating their execution details; - `run_authorization_cid` binds the Host's current allow or approved decision for that exact Prepared Invocation; - `run_definition_cid` binds the immutable definition of one durable Run, including its initial captured input artifact set ([Run admission and identity](execution.md#run-admission)); - `invocation_cid` binds Program Definition, parameter-values, and Check Environment identities to the exact captured observation evidence ([Capture, execution, and replay](execution.md#capture-and-replay));
